## Plate Driving Forces and Motion Rates
The outer layer of Earth, the lithosphere, is not one solid shell. It is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates. These plates float on the asthenosphere, a ductile (slowly flowing) layer beneath them.
Why do plates move? Three driving forces act together: mantle convection (slow churning of the mantle), slab pull (a sinking plate edge pulling the rest), and ridge push (raised ridges pushing plates outward). Think of it like a k-pop dance formation: each dancer moves because of pushes and pulls from the group, and the whole pattern shifts in a coordinated way.
How fast do plates move? Relative motion is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). Think of it like birdwatching: a bird gliding across the sky seems slow, but over hours it travels far. Plates are the same: a few centimetres each year becomes thousands of kilometres over millions of years.
There are three types of plate boundary, defined by relative motion: Divergent → plates pull apart → normal-fault earthquakes, shallow depths Convergent → plates collide → thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow Transform → plates slide past → strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate
Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries instead of happening anywhere? Four reasons: 1. Stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction; strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. 2. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. 3. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. 4. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
A common wrong idea: earthquakes happen at random places on Earth. This fails because the four clustering mechanisms all act at plate edges, where plates interact. The correct view is the key point: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. In other words, the pattern of quakes maps out where and how plates meet.

## The Seismic Cycle at a Convergent Margin
At a convergent margin, one plate slides beneath another. The seismic cycle is the repeating pattern of how strain (stored elastic energy) builds and is released there.
The cycle has four stages. Interseismic: the locked zone accumulates strain over decades to centuries. Coseismic: sudden slip releases the stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. Postseismic: afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years. Preseismic: possible warning signals such as foreshocks and slow slip may appear before a large event.
In words: strain builds slowly, then is released suddenly, then stress is redistributed. As a chain: interseismic (strain builds) → coseismic (sudden slip) → postseismic (afterslip + viscoelastic relaxation) → possible preseismic signals before the next event.
Seismic gap theory says a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle is a candidate for a future large event. Think of it like a k-pop dance routine where one section has not yet been performed: that missing section is where the next performance will happen. In the same way, the unruptured segment is where the next large earthquake is expected.

Intermediate to deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of the subducting slab. A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.

## Implications for Seismic Hazard Assessment
Seismic hazard assessment asks where large earthquakes are likely next. The material gives a four-step checklist. First, identify the plate boundary type for the region of interest. Second, obtain relative plate velocities in cm yr⁻¹ from global models such as MORVEL or NUVEL-1A.
Third, map earthquake depths in km to infer the seismogenic thickness (the depth range where faults can store and release strain). Fourth, evaluate coupling and seismic gap status for probabilistic hazard.
Seismic gap theory: segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. Think of it like a k-pop dance routine where one section has never been performed live; that untested section is where the next surprise is most likely.
GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities (cm yr⁻¹) to refine coupling models. Coupling means how tightly the plate interface is locked between earthquakes. Depth distribution of seismicity informs the likely rupture extent and tsunami potential.
The rates matter: the Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to North America at about 5 cm yr⁻¹, and the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at about 8 cm yr⁻¹. These rates explain the high frequency of large earthquakes along the Circum-Pacific Ring of Fire.
Depth patterns differ by boundary type. Shallow events (≤ 10 km) dominate divergent ridges and transform faults. Intermediate–deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has stages: interseismic (locked zone accumulates strain, decades to centuries), coseismic (sudden slip releases stored elastic energy, seconds to minutes), postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation, months to years), and possible preseismic signals (foreshocks, slow slip).
In words: unruptured, strongly coupled segments are the prime hazard candidates. As a picture: boundary type → velocity (MORVEL/NUVEL-1A) ↓ depth map → seismogenic thickness ↓ coupling + gap status → probabilistic hazard → tsunami potential
